title: What You Would Build
principle: Being able to say how you would find out you were wrong is the whole thing.

t: Last one. You have taken living things apart for long enough. What would you make?
The final build. Everything from here is yours to specify — and the design will be tested on the reasoning rather than on the biology.
sub: And more importantly: why that, and how would anyone know if it worked?
A design nobody can check is not a design. It is an announcement.

question: What separates a good design from an impressive one?
What distinguishes a defensible design from a merely capable one?
options: You can say how you would find out that you were wrong
It has never been tried before
stages.outcome: You can say how you would find out that you were wrong
note: Commit. Every measurement in this whole curriculum had this property; that is why they were worth doing.

t: Build your design. Any part fits any slot, so the marking is entirely on you.
Assemble what a defensible proposal requires, then five tests. Nothing here checks whether the organism would work — only whether you could justify building it.

parts.label: Something in biology that could do it
A way to tell whether it worked

label: Why anyone should want this at all
The part that has to actually be true about living things
What result would prove you wrong
What you would do if it went badly

name: Say what it is for
Purpose
pass: There is a problem, and this is aimed at it.
A stated problem makes benefit assessable and success definable.
fail: Without a stated problem there is no criterion for success, so nothing can be evaluated.

name: Say how it would work
Mechanism
pass: A real mechanism, of the kind you have been taking apart all the way through.
A specified mechanism grounded in known biology, which makes the proposal checkable by someone else.
fail: A wish with no machinery under it.
A proposal with no mechanism cannot be criticised, which is a defect rather than a strength.

name: Say how you would know
Test
pass: You named a result that would prove you wrong.
A falsifiable prediction. This is the rung the whole curriculum has been rehearsing.
fail: Nothing could ever show this was a bad idea, which is the problem with it.
A design compatible with every outcome makes no claim about the world and cannot be evaluated by anyone, including you.

name: Say how to stop it
Reversibility
pass: If it goes wrong, there is a way back.
A defined off-switch — containment, dependency, or a bounded deployment — keeps the required standard of evidence proportionate.
fail: It works, and if it turns out to be a mistake, that is permanent.
Irreversibility raises the standard of proof rather than merely warranting more care. Design the stop before the start.

name: Say who you asked
Authority
pass: The people who have to live with it were asked, and agreed.
Those bearing the risk consented, or a body with standing to decide for them authorised it.
fail: A careful, testable, reversible plan that nobody agreed to.
The last rung is not a formality. It is the objection that survives after every technical answer has been given.

win: A reason, a mechanism, a test, a way back, and permission. That is a design you can defend.

All five. Note what was never assessed: whether the organism would work. A proposal that clears these five and then fails at the bench is an ordinary scientific result. One that works and clears none of them is the thing this world has been warning you about.
lose: Read which test failed — it names what your design is missing.
Each failed trial names an unmet requirement. Reassign and re-test.

t: Being able to say how you would find out you were wrong is the whole thing. Everything else was practice.
A design is defensible when it states a purpose, a mechanism, a disconfirming test, a route back and a source of permission. Four of those five are not biology.
This is also, in reverse, how everything in these six worlds was established. Somebody stated what they thought was happening, said what would be observed if they were wrong, and went and looked.

It is worth seeing the pattern whole now that you have done it a hundred times. You changed one thing at a time and watched what moved. You ran the model before you trusted the story about it. You found the cases where the maximum lost to the middle, where the fastest copy was not the best one, where removing one animal changed three others. Nothing in that method is about biology in particular — which is why it transfers, and why it is the thing actually worth taking away from here.
sub: You have done this a hundred times already. This is just the name for it.
Every simulation you ran was a version of this: change one thing, and see what moves.
The method is older and more general than any of the content it was used on here.

And it is not a claim that this method answers every question worth asking. It answers questions about how things behave, extremely well, and it has nothing to say about what any of it is for. Knowing precisely where the method stops is part of using it honestly — and that boundary, rather than any particular finding, is where the most interesting arguments in this whole curriculum have been.

q: What is the most important thing to be able to say about your own idea?
Which element of a proposal makes it assessable by anyone else?
Why is disconfirmability the load-bearing requirement rather than plausibility?
options: What would happen if it were wrong, and how you would find out
That it has never been done before
That you are confident it will work
why: Anyone can be sure. Being able to say what would change your mind is what makes an idea worth listening to, and it is what you have been practising the whole way through.
A stated disconfirming result makes the claim checkable independently of the person making it. Novelty and confidence are properties of the proposer; a test is a property of the proposal.

Because a plausible claim compatible with every outcome forbids nothing and therefore says nothing about the world. Disconfirmability is what makes a proposal a claim at all — and it is also what makes being wrong survivable, which is the practical reason to insist on it.

t: Every single thing you have looked at here is still being argued about by somebody.

The measurements are firm and the interpretations are not settled, in every world you have played through: what the first cell needed, how much a genome can change, whether a rock from Mars ever held anything, what a resurrected animal is. You now know enough to follow those arguments, to tell which parts are measurement and which are interpretation, and to ask the question that matters most in any of them — what would change your mind? That is not the end of this. It is the point at which you stop needing it.
